claim: Retrotransposons (RTEs) have been postulated to reactivate with age and contribute to aging through activated innate immune response and inflammation.
source: Retrotransposons (RTEs) have been postulated to reactivate with age and contribute to aging through activated innate immune response and inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature and scientific consensus on RTE reactivation and aging.

claim: There is no observed correlation between RTE activity and chronological age.
source: Despite no observed correlation between RTE activity and chronological age, the expression of most RTE classes and families except short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) correlated with biological age-associated gene signature scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of transcriptomic datasets presented in the manuscript, as shown in Figure 2a and related text.

claim: The expression of most RTE classes and families except SINEs correlated with biological age-associated gene signature scores.
source: Despite no observed correlation between RTE activity and chronological age, the expression of most RTE classes and families except short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) correlated with biological age-associated gene signature scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between RTE expression and BAR gene signature scores shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression of SINEs was linked to upregulated DNA repair pathways in multiple cohorts.
source: Strikingly, we found that the expression of SINEs was linked to upregulated DNA repair pathways in multiple cohorts.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: DNA hypomethylation occurs with aging.
source: We also observed DNA hypomethylation with aging and the significant increase in RTE expression level in hypomethylated RTEs except for SINEs.
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis across multiple cohorts shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a significant increase in RTE expression level in hypomethylated RTEs except for SINEs.
source: We also observed DNA hypomethylation with aging and the significant increase in RTE expression level in hypomethylated RTEs except for SINEs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis between methylation and expression levels shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Plasma cells play a role in aging mediated by RTEs.
source: Additionally, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis suggested a role for plasma cells in aging mediated by RTEs.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5a-f.

claim: RTEs are categorized into DNA transposons and RTEs, which depend on cDNA intermediates to function.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are genetic elements that can move within the genome and are categorized into DNA transposons and RTEs, which depend on cDNA intermediates to function.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about transposable element classification.

claim: RTEs include three classes: endogenous retrovirus long terminal repeats (LTRs), and long and short interspersed nuclear elements, known as LINEs and SINEs, respectively.
source: RTEs include three classes: endogenous retrovirus long terminal repeats (LTRs), and long and short interspersed nuclear elements, known as LINEs and SINEs, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RTE classification.

claim: LINEs and SINEs employ target-primed reverse transcription for genome integration.
source: LINEs and SINEs employ target-primed reverse transcription for genome integration, with SINEs depending on the proteins encoded by LINEs (Bourque et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bourque et al., 2018.

claim: SINEs depend on the proteins encoded by LINEs for genome integration.
source: LINEs and SINEs employ target-primed reverse transcription for genome integration, with SINEs depending on the proteins encoded by LINEs (Bourque et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bourque et al., 2018.

claim: Most of the RTE sequences are dormant in the host genome.
source: Although most of the RTE sequences are dormant in the host genome, they continue to play vital roles in human evolution and physiology (Gorbunova et al., 2014; Gorbunova et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gorbunova et al., 2014 and 2021.

claim: RTEs continue to play vital roles in human evolution and physiology.
source: Although most of the RTE sequences are dormant in the host genome, they continue to play vital roles in human evolution and physiology (Gorbunova et al., 2014; Gorbunova et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gorbunova et al., 2014 and 2021.

claim: RTEs are silenced through heterochromatinization and DNA methylation in the early developmental stages as part of the host defense mechanism.
source: RTEs are silenced through heterochromatinization and DNA methylation in the early developmental stages as part of the host defense mechanism (Gorbunova et al., 2021; Van Meter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gorbunova et al., 2021 and Van Meter et al., 2014.

claim: Increased RTE activity that occurs with aging can lead to genome instability and activation of DNA damage pathways.
source: However, increased RTE activity that occurs with aging can lead to genome instability and activation of DNA damage pathways (Van Meter et al., 2014; Tsurumi and Li, 2012; De Cecco et al., 2013b; Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Van Meter et al., 2014; Tsurumi and Li, 2012; De Cecco et al., 2013b; Wood et al., 2016.

claim: Accumulation of cytoplasmic RTE cDNAs detected in aging organisms and senescent cells can activate type I interferon (IFN-I) response and inflammation.
source: Additionally, accumulation of cytoplasmic RTE cDNAs detected in aging organisms and senescent cells can activate type I interferon (IFN-I) response and inflammation (Gorbunova et al., 2021; Van Meter et al., 2014; De Cecco et al., 2019; Simon et al., 2019; De Cecco et al., 2013a), that contributes to inflammaging (Franceschi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Gorbunova et al., 2021; Van Meter et al., 2014; De Cecco et al., 2019; Simon et al., 2019; De Cecco et al., 2013a; Franceschi et al., 2000.

claim: Accumulation of cytoplasmic RTE cDNAs contributes to inflammaging.
source: Additionally, accumulation of cytoplasmic RTE cDNAs detected in aging organisms and senescent cells can activate type I interferon (IFN-I) response and inflammation (Gorbunova et al., 2021; Van Meter et al., 2014; De Cecco et al., 2019; Simon et al., 2019; De Cecco et al., 2013a), that contributes to inflammaging (Franceschi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franceschi et al., 2000.

claim: Chromatin remodeling and cellular senescence contribute partially to the RTE reactivation.
source: Furthermore, chromatin remodeling and cellular senescence also contribute partially to the RTE reactivation (De Cecco et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to De Cecco et al., 2013a.

claim: Cellular senescence is a non-proliferative state elicited by stress factors such as DNA damage and is closely intertwined with inflammation and aging.
source: Cellular senescence is a non-proliferative state elicited by stress factors such as DNA damage and is closely intertwined with inflammation and aging (Gorgoulis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gorgoulis et al., 2019.

claim: Senescent cells promote inflammation and senescence in other cells, including immune cells, through the expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: Through the expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), senescent cells promote inflammation and senescence in other cells, including immune cells, leading to a compromised immune system and a vicious cycle of inflammation (Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Coppé et al., 2010.

claim: SASP expression leads to a compromised immune system and a vicious cycle of inflammation.
source: Through the expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), senescent cells promote inflammation and senescence in other cells, including immune cells, leading to a compromised immune system and a vicious cycle of inflammation (Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Coppé et al., 2010.

claim: No significant relationship (p-value < 0.05) is found between chronological age and expressions of the three RTE classes across the MESA, GARP, and GTP datasets.
source: Strikingly, no significant relationship (p-value < 0.05) is found between chronological age and expressions of the three RTE classes across the datasets (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Apart from a weak correlation observed between a few RTE families and chronological age, no strong relation exists between chronological age and expression of RTE families across the three cohorts.
source: Similarly, apart from a weak correlation observed between a few RTE families and chronological age, we could not identify any strong relation between chronological age and expression of RTE families across the three cohorts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No significant difference in RTE expression was found in any cell type between young (aged 25–29) and old (aged 62–70) groups in scRNA-seq data of PBMCs.
source: When comparing the RTE expression of the young (aged 25–29, n=11) group with the old (aged 62–70, n=10) group, we could not find any significant difference or trend in any cell types between the two groups (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: No statistically significant correlation was observed between chronological age and expression of RTE classes or families in RNA-seq data on healthy human PBMC.
source: We did not observe any statistically significant correlation between chronological age and expression of RTE classes or families (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: RTE expression did not correlate with chronological aging across the microarray, scRNA-seq, and RNA-seq datasets.
source: Overall, RTE expression did not correlate with chronological aging across the microarray, scRNA-seq, and RNA-seq datasets.
evidence: This claim is a summary of multiple analyses across different data types.

claim: Positive correlations were observed between the expressions of LINEs and LTRs and BAR gene signature scores across three datasets.
source: Positive correlations were observed between the expressions of LINEs and LTRs and BAR gene signature scores across three datasets, while inverse correlation was present between the expression of SINEs and these scores in the PBMC samples from the GARP cohort (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: Inverse correlation was present between the expression of SINEs and BAR gene signature scores in the PBMC samples from the GARP cohort.
source: Positive correlations were observed between the expressions of LINEs and LTRs and BAR gene signature scores across three datasets, while inverse correlation was present between the expression of SINEs and these scores in the PBMC samples from the GARP cohort (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: The strongest positive correlation with BAR scores was observed in L1, ERVK, and ERVL in the GARP cohort.
source: In the GARP cohort, the strongest positive correlation with BAR scores was observed in L1, ERVK, and ERVL.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The expressions of Alu and MIR of SINE, L2, and ERV1 were inversely correlated with BAR signature scores in the GARP cohort.
source: By contrast, the expressions of Alu and MIR of SINE, L2, and ERV1 were inversely correlated with BAR signature scores in the GARP cohort (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: There is an overall trend of increased scores of BAR gene signatures in high versus low LINE and LTR expression groups across the datasets.
source: Across the datasets, there is an overall trend of increased scores of BAR gene signatures in high versus low LINE and LTR expression groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The most significant increase in BAR gene signatures was found for SASP and senescence and to a lesser extent for inflammaging signatures.
source: In fact, amongst all gene sets, we found the most significant increase for SASP and senescence and to a lesser extent for inflammaging signatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: There is a significant correlation between IFN-I signature score and expression of LINE and LTR classes and most of their families (p-value <0.01) in RNA-seq PBMC data.
source: Interestingly, when we examined RNA-seq PBMC data, we found that there is a significant correlation between IFN-I signature score and expression of LINE and LTR classes and most of their families (p-value <0.01), but such a significant correlation did not exist between IFN-I score and SINE class and Alu family (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: No significant correlation exists between IFN-I score and SINE class and Alu family in RNA-seq PBMC data.
source: Interestingly, when we examined RNA-seq PBMC data, we found that there is a significant correlation between IFN-I signature score and expression of LINE and LTR classes and most of their families (p-value <0.01), but such a significant correlation did not exist between IFN-I score and SINE class and Alu family (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: A significant fraction of gene sets related to DNA repair were downregulated in the group of monocyte samples highly expressing LINE and LTR classes.
source: We found that a significant fraction of gene sets related to DNA repair were downregulated in the group of monocyte samples (MESA cohort) highly expressing LINE and LTR classes but upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples (MESA and GARP cohorts, respectively) highly expressing SINEs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gene sets related to DNA repair were upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples highly expressing SINEs.
source: We found that a significant fraction of gene sets related to DNA repair were downregulated in the group of monocyte samples (MESA cohort) highly expressing LINE and LTR classes but upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples (MESA and GARP cohorts, respectively) highly expressing SINEs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There is a unique increase in DNA repair activity in the monocytes of the cohort with high Alu expression.
source: At the family level, there is a unique increase in DNA repair activity in the monocytes of the cohort with high Alu expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: DNA repair pathways are upregulated in groups highly expressing L2, ERV1, Alu, and MIR in the PBMC samples of the GARP dataset.
source: In the PBMC samples of the GARP dataset, DNA repair pathways are upregulated in groups highly expressing L2, ERV1, Alu, and MIR, while most of the other RTE classes demonstrate decreased DNA repair activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Most of the other RTE classes demonstrate decreased DNA repair activity in the PBMC samples of the GARP dataset.
source: In the PBMC samples of the GARP dataset, DNA repair pathways are upregulated in groups highly expressing L2, ERV1, Alu, and MIR, while most of the other RTE classes demonstrate decreased DNA repair activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The inflammatory response is upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples of groups expressing LINE and LTR classes and families at high levels.
source: In contrast, the inflammatory response is upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples of groups expressing LINE and LTR classes and families at high levels, and such upregulation is less common in SINE (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Upregulation of inflammatory response is less common in SINE.
source: In contrast, the inflammatory response is upregulated in the monocyte and PBMC samples of groups expressing LINE and LTR classes and families at high levels, and such upregulation is less common in SINE (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: SINE might contribute to aging via genome instability instead of inflammation that is associated with LINE and LTR activities.
source: These observations provide insight into the perpetuating contrast between SINE versus LINE and LTR observed in our analysis, as SINE might contribute to aging via genome instability instead of inflammation that is associated with LINE and LTR activities.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the GSVA analysis results.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between the methylation level of RTEs and chronological age across all RTE classes and families in the WB and monocytes.
source: Our analysis showed an inverse correlation between the methylation level of RTEs and chronological age across all RTE classes and families in the WB and monocytes (Figure 4a–b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4a-b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed trend of demethylation of RTE with age is in line with previous reports of demethylation of RTE with age in gene-poor regions.
source: This observed trend is in line with previous reports of demethylation of RTE with age in gene-poor regions (Tsurumi and Li, 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Hannum et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsurumi and Li, 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Hannum et al., 2013.

claim: The DNA methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs significantly decreased in groups of high LINE and LTR expressions, respectively.
source: The DNA methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs significantly decreased in groups of high LINE and LTR expressions, respectively, but SINEs and the satellite repeats (as negative control) did not display the same pattern (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: SINEs and the satellite repeats did not display the same pattern of decreased methylation in high expression groups.
source: The DNA methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs significantly decreased in groups of high LINE and LTR expressions, respectively, but SINEs and the satellite repeats (as negative control) did not display the same pattern (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: LINE families, MIR, and LTR families except ERVK displayed lower levels of methylation in higher expression groups.
source: LINE families, MIR, and LTR families except ERVK displayed lower levels of methylation in higher expression groups, while such patterns was absent in Alu, CR1, and ERVl (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pattern of lower methylation in higher expression groups was absent in Alu, CR1, and ERVl.
source: LINE families, MIR, and LTR families except ERVK displayed lower levels of methylation in higher expression groups, while such patterns was absent in Alu, CR1, and ERVl (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The DNA methylation level of SINEs positively correlated with the methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs.
source: Although the DNA methylation level of SINEs positively correlated with the methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs, the expression of SINEs was not significantly correlated with the expression levels of other RTE classes (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The expression of SINEs was not significantly correlated with the expression levels of other RTE classes.
source: Although the DNA methylation level of SINEs positively correlated with the methylation levels of LINEs and LTRs, the expression of SINEs was not significantly correlated with the expression levels of other RTE classes (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: DNA methylation plays a dispensable role for SINE silencing in monocytes.
source: This result also suggests a dispensable role of DNA methylation for SINE silencing in monocytes, which is in line with previous studies showing SINEs are not derepressed by deletion of DNA methyltransferases or treatment with DNA demethylating agents and are primarily regulated by histone modifications (Varshney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data and is supported by citation to Varshney et al., 2015.

claim: SINEs are not derepressed by deletion of DNA methyltransferases or treatment with DNA demethylating agents and are primarily regulated by histone modifications.
source: This result also suggests a dispensable role of DNA methylation for SINE silencing in monocytes, which is in line with previous studies showing SINEs are not derepressed by deletion of DNA methyltransferases or treatment with DNA demethylating agents and are primarily regulated by histone modifications (Varshney et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Varshney et al., 2015.

claim: Plasma cells consistently demonstrate significantly elevated RTE expression in cells of high SASP expression.
source: Among the 25 annotated cell types, plasma cells consistently demonstrate significantly elevated RTE expression in cells of high SASP expression that is not observed in the other cell types (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Increased LINE and SINE expressions were observed in the plasma cells of the samples with high inflammatory chemokines and inflammaging gene signature scores.
source: Increased LINE and SINE expressions were also observed in the plasma cells of the samples with high inflammatory chemokines and inflammaging gene signature scores (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: Elevated RTE expression was seen in the groups with high inflammatory cytokines and senescence but not IFN-I scores, although not statistically significant.
source: Although not statistically significant, elevated RTE expression was also seen in the groups with high inflammatory cytokines and senescence but not IFN-I scores (Figure 5d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5d-f.

claim: Plasma cells might play an important role in the process in which reactivation of RTEs regulates aging.
source: Overall, this finding indicates that plasma cells might play an important role in the process in which reactivation of RTEs regulates aging.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Supercentenarians demonstrated decreased RTE expression in the natural killer (NK) cells, B-cells, T-cells, monocytes, and dendritic cells compared with the control group.
source: Compared with the control group, the supercentenarians demonstrated decreased RTE expression in the natural killer (NK) cells, B-cells, T-cells, monocytes, and dendritic cells (Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both T cell types showed decreased LINE expression in supercentenarians.
source: Both T cell types showed decreased LINE expression, while the noncytotoxic cluster, TC1, showed slightly decreased LTR expression, and the expanding cytotoxic T cells, TC2, showed decreased SINE expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The noncytotoxic cluster, TC1, showed slightly decreased LTR expression in supercentenarians.
source: Both T cell types showed decreased LINE expression, while the noncytotoxic cluster, TC1, showed slightly decreased LTR expression, and the expanding cytotoxic T cells, TC2, showed decreased SINE expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The expanding cytotoxic T cells, TC2, showed decreased SINE expression in supercentenarians.
source: Both T cell types showed decreased LINE expression, while the noncytotoxic cluster, TC1, showed slightly decreased LTR expression, and the expanding cytotoxic T cells, TC2, showed decreased SINE expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The cytotoxic T cells demonstrated an increased level of inflammatory cytokines and inflammaging gene signature scores in supercentenarians.
source: On the other hand, the cytotoxic T cells also demonstrated an increased level of inflammatory cytokines and inflammaging gene signature scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The NK cells displayed higher senescence and SASP scores in the supercentenarians while demonstrating decreased LINE and SINE expressions.
source: In addition, the NK cells displayed higher senescence and SASP scores in the supercentenarians while demonstrating decreased LINE and SINE expressions (Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplements 5–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplements 5–6.

claim: Inflammatory activity in cytotoxic T cells and increased senescence in the NK cells are not associated with the activation of RTEs in supercentenarians.
source: Overall, this result reveals inflammatory activity in cytotoxic T cells and increased senescence in the NK cells that are not associated with the activation of RTEs in supercentenarians.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: The expression of RTEs is significantly reduced in most of the immune cell types in supercentenarians.
source: By contrast, the expression of RTEs is significantly reduced in most of the immune cell types in supercentenarians.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The role of RTEs in aging has not been studied in a systematic manner with large, non-cancerous human cohorts across RTE categories before this study.
source: The role of RTEs in aging has been studied extensively but not in a systematic manner with large, non-cancerous human cohorts across RTE categories before this study.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Current understanding of the relationship between RTEs and aging are largely conducted in vitro or in model organisms that might not apply to humans due to intraspecies differences.
source: Current understanding of the relationship between RTEs and aging are largely conducted in vitro or in model organisms Wood et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2019; LaRocca et al., 2020 that might not apply to humans due to intraspecies differences (Venuto and Bourque, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wood et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2019; LaRocca et al., 2020; Venuto and Bourque, 2018.

claim: The link of RTEs to aging in non-cancerous human cohorts has not been studied systematically in large cohorts.
source: Moreover, the link of RTEs to aging in non-cancerous human cohorts has not been studied systematically in large cohorts.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Chronological aging is not significantly linked with RTE reactivation.
source: We combined bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data to examine the relationship between RTE expression versus chronological and biological aging, demonstrating that chronological aging is not significantly linked with RTE reactivation.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings from multiple analyses.

claim: LTR and LINE expressions are positively correlated with the BAR gene signature scores.
source: In this process, we discovered that LTR and LINE expressions are positively correlated with the BAR gene signature scores.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings from correlation analyses.

claim: The SINE expression demonstrates an inverse correlation with BAR scores in the PBMC samples and no significant relationship in the WB.
source: However, in contrast, the SINE expression demonstrates an inverse correlation with BAR scores in the PBMC samples and no significant relationship in the WB.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings from correlation analyses.

claim: The absence of a positive correlation between BAR scores and SINE expression might be linked to the upregulation of DNA repair pathways in groups with high SINE and Alu expressions.
source: We suspect the absence of a positive correlation between BAR scores and SINE expression might be linked to the same discrepancy observed in the GSVA analysis, in which DNA repair pathways are upregulated in the groups of cases with high SINE and Alu expressions.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the GSVA analysis results.

claim: Reactivation of SINE, particularly Alu, might lead to DNA damage, a hallmark of aging.
source: This result suggests that reactivation of SINE, particularly Alu, might lead to DNA damage, a hallmark of aging.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the GSVA analysis results.

claim: Alu is not studied as extensively as L1 from the LINE class.
source: Although SINEs compose up to 13% of the human genome, and Alu elements make up the largest family of human mobile elements, Alu is not studied as extensively as L1 from the LINE class (Bourque et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bourque et al., 2018 and general knowledge.

claim: The groups of cases with high LINE and LTR expressions have upregulation of the pathways related to the inflammatory response.
source: In contrast, the groups of cases with high LINE and LTR expressions have upregulation of the pathways related to the inflammatory response, which is in line with the previous findings from human and model organisms (Gorbunova et al., 2021; LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis and citations to Gorbunova et al., 2021; LaRocca et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanisms of aging and age-related diseases (ARDs) converge on inflammaging.
source: The mechanisms of aging and age-related diseases (ARDs) converge on inflammaging (Franceschi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franceschi et al., 2018.

claim: Previous studies have shown RTE's pathogenetic role in ARDs including neurodegenerative diseases through elevation of DNA damage and genome instability.
source: Previous studies have shown RTE's pathogenetic role in ARDs including neurodegenerative diseases through elevation of DNA damage and genome instability (Kaneko et al., 2011; Andrenacci et al., 2020; Fukuda et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaneko et al., 2011; Andrenacci et al., 2020; Fukuda et al., 2021.

claim: SINE expression inversely correlated with the BAR signature scores in the PBMCs of osteoarthritis patients.
source: SINE expression inversely correlated with the BAR signature scores in the PBMCs of osteoarthritis patients, while a positive correlation is observed in monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis in the GARP cohort.

claim: A positive correlation between SINE expression and BAR signature scores is observed in monocytes.
source: SINE expression inversely correlated with the BAR signature scores in the PBMCs of osteoarthritis patients, while a positive correlation is observed in monocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis in the MESA cohort.

claim: A discrepant upregulation of DNA repair pathways is seen in the osteoarthritis cohorts expressing higher level L2, ERV1, Alu, and MIR.
source: Moreover, a discrepant upregulation of DNA repair pathways is seen in the osteoarthritis cohorts expressing higher level L2, ERV1, Alu, and MIR.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSVA analysis in the GARP cohort.

claim: The methylation levels of all three RTE classes decrease with chronological age.
source: The methylation levels of all three RTE classes decrease with chronological age in our analysis, and the RTE expression is in inverse correlation with the methylation level in LINE and LTR but not in SINE.
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The RTE expression is in inverse correlation with the methylation level in LINE and LTR but not in SINE.
source: The methylation levels of all three RTE classes decrease with chronological age in our analysis, and the RTE expression is in inverse correlation with the methylation level in LINE and LTR but not in SINE.
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation and expression correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: RTE sequences are repressed via DNA methylation and heterochromatinization.
source: RTE sequences are repressed via DNA methylation and heterochromatinization (Deniz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Deniz et al., 2019.

claim: In the aging process, surveillance of transcriptional regulators such as SIRT6 wanes, leading to hypomethylation and heterochromatin reduction.
source: In the aging process, surveillance of transcriptional regulators such as SIRT6 wanes, leading to hypomethylation and heterochromatin reduction (Van Meter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Van Meter et al., 2014.

claim: L1 has been identified to be repressed through DNA methylation.
source: L1 has been identified to be repressed through DNA methylation (Woodcock et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Woodcock et al., 1997.

claim: SINE has been suggested to be predominantly regulated by histone modification, and loss of DNA methylation has little effect on the transcription of SINEs.
source: However, SINE has been suggested to be predominantly regulated by histone modification, and loss of DNA methylation has little effect on the transcription of SINEs (Varshney et al., 2015), as reflected in our analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Varshney et al., 2015.

claim: Expression microarray has been successfully employed to study the expression of RTEs.
